title: 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: We do not expect further funding for the next 12 to 18 months period at all and thereafter we expect the business generate cash on its own.
epigraph.author: Manish Poddar, Group CFO, Greaves Cotton, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: The ten-year record of Greaves is two stories in one set of accounts. The first is an engine business that earned 11–15% margins through FY20, was hit by COVID, new emission rules, a chip shortage and a metal-price spike, and has climbed back to a 13–14% standalone margin [8][6]. The second is an electric-vehicle subsidiary, acquired in stages from 2018, that has absorbed cash in every year and lost ₹477.32 crore to a single subsidy provision in FY24 [8]. The consolidated statements blend the two. This chapter pulls them apart using the core-versus-GEML disclosure Greaves began in FY27 [1].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated ten-year record, FY15 to H1 FY27 (₹ crore; EBITDA is operating profit before depreciation and interest; net profit includes minority share; borrowings include lease liabilities; Screener consolidated table cross-checked to annual reports)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue doubled over eleven years, about 6.6% a year (derived from ₹1,698 crore and ₹3,437 crore), but EBITDA rose only from ₹192 crore to ₹239 crore [60]. Cash splits the table in two: operating cash flow was positive every year to FY21 and totalled ₹1,243 crore, then summed to −₹334 crore over FY22–FY26 (derived from the rows) [60][9][8][6]. FY25 EBITDA is ₹136 crore in the company deck and ₹137 crore in the aggregator; we use the aggregator figure for consistency [4][60].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated profit and loss, FY15 to trailing twelve months to September 2026 (₹ crore; Screener consolidated table)
web_blocks.takeaway: Margin peaked at 15% in FY17, fell to 1.5% in FY22 and recovered to 7% in FY26 [60]. Below that line three costs grew while profit did not: depreciation from ₹48 crore to ₹109 crore, interest from ₹2 crore to ₹26 crore (₹43 crore trailing), and tax, which exceeded pre-tax profit in FY25 (109%) because GEML's losses do not offset profits elsewhere in the group, our inference rather than a company statement [6]. The FY24 loss of ₹367 crore is the FAME provision. FY16's other income of ₹138 crore lifted pre-tax profit above operating profit; our evidence does not itemise it.

web_blocks.caption: Margin bridge: core, GEML and consolidated EBITDA (₹ crore; core and GEML from the Q2 FY27 investor deck; residual is our subtraction and includes the lender and eliminations)
web_blocks.takeaway: Between H1 FY26 and H1 FY27 group EBITDA rose ₹21 crore: GEML improved by ₹15 crore, the residual by ₹12 crore, and the core fell by ₹6 crore despite 20% higher revenue [1][60]. The consolidated margin therefore held near 6% for two opposite reasons, a weakening core and a recovering subsidiary. The core margin fell because raw materials rose from 63.9% to 67.8% of revenue (H1) while OEM contracts reprice only with a lag [1][24]. Peer data say this is industry-wide, not Greaves-specific: Kirloskar Oil Engines' standalone margin fell from 14.0% to 11.0% in the same quarter [81].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated balance sheet, March 2015 to September 2026 (₹ crore; Screener consolidated table)
web_blocks.takeaway: Net worth (equity capital plus reserves) was ₹823 crore in FY15 and ₹1,431 crore in FY26. The step-up came in FY23, when reserves went from ₹703 crore to ₹1,540 crore as Abdul Latif Jameel invested ₹1,170.81 crore in GEML, not from retained profit [9][60]. Reserves have since slipped to ₹1,319 crore after the FAME loss, dividends and minority losses. Fixed assets doubled from ₹369 crore to ₹825 crore in FY24, coinciding with the Excel purchase [8]. About 70% of total assets at September 2026 sit in “other assets” (receivables, inventory, loans, deposits), so working capital matters more than the factory count.

web_blocks.caption: Why borrowings rose: Mar-25 to Mar-26 to Sep-26 (₹ crore; filings; Screener “borrowings” = borrowings plus leases)
rows: Greaves Finance: NCDs 108.52, NBFC loans 53.86, bank term loans 30.37, secured on vehicle-finance receivables
Not split; ₹185 crore of 10.5% NCDs raised in H1 FY27
Loans from erstwhile Bestway directors (24% penal rate if overdue)
web_blocks.takeaway: The debt did not fund the engine business. At least ₹192.75 crore of the March 2026 total is match-funded: the loans are secured on, and repaid from, the EV lender's receivables, and the lender is rated IND A− [6][97]. Most of the rest funded GEML's working capital. The core (Greaves plus Excel) held ₹150 crore of cash against ₹40 crore of debt, a net ₹110 crore of cash [62]. Leases rose about ₹40 crore on ₹59.37 crore of new right-of-use assets, which the aggregator figure hides [6]. Consolidated cash and investments of ₹606 crore exceed borrowings of ₹513 crore, but part of that cash sits in GEML and GFL after the rights issue [1].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated cash flow, FY15 to FY26 (₹ crore; Screener consolidated table; free cash flow is operating cash flow less capital spending)
web_blocks.takeaway: FY15–FY21 delivered ₹1,243 crore of operating cash (sum of the rows) and about ₹1,043 crore of free cash flow (Screener's free cash flow line, including FY15 and FY16 rows that the table below does not show). FY22–FY26 delivered −₹334 crore and −₹614 crore. Outside money bridged the gap: financing brought in ₹210 crore in FY22 and ₹889 crore in FY23, the latter around the ALJ investment [60][9]. The CFO-to-EBITDA row shows conversion above 100% in FY15, FY16, FY18 and FY21 and below zero in FY22–FY24; the FY26 reading of 47% is better, but the lending book explains the rest, as the next paragraph shows.

web_blocks.text: Cash conversion. Four items explain most of the five-year shortfall. In FY23, ₹332.50 crore went into “other assets”, reflecting a FAME subsidy receivable of ₹371.52 crore at March 2023 [9][8]. In FY24, ₹114.19 crore of tax was paid on the Pune land-sale gain [8]. In FY26, ₹242.21 crore went into other assets, mostly the EV lender's loan book [6]. In H1 FY27, ₹205.08 crore did the same, as non-current loans rose from ₹80.66 crore to ₹286.57 crore [2]. Adding back the first two to the five-year total gives −₹334.42 crore plus ₹332.50 crore plus ₹114.19 crore, about ₹112 crore, still thin against ₹619 crore of EBITDA over the same years (₹25, 127, 91, 137 and 239 crore). H1 FY27 operating cash flow of −₹211.82 crore becomes about −₹6.74 crore before the loan-book line, and the ₹140.87 crore inventory build was partly offset by ₹98.34 crore more owed to suppliers [2]. Standalone operating cash flow was −₹14 crore against +₹73.7 crore a year earlier, so the core is not immune [2].

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital days and ROCE, FY15 to FY26 (Screener consolidated ratios; days are on sales or cost as the aggregator defines them)
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days (DSO, days to collect from customers) improved from 50 to 37; inventory days (DIO, days stock is held) rose from 34 to 50; payable days (DPO, days taken to pay suppliers) rose from 46 to 92, peaking at 120 in FY21. Because suppliers now fund more days than stock and customers combined, the cash conversion cycle is −6 days against +37 in FY15 [60]. That works only while suppliers stay willing: payables rose from ₹580.85 crore to ₹689.56 crore in H1 FY27 while inventory rose faster [2]. ROCE (profit before interest and tax over capital employed) follows margin: 18–28% through FY20, 3% in FY21, −1% in FY22, 10% in FY26 [60].

web_blocks.text: Return drivers. Our own arithmetic on FY26 gives a ROCE of about 7.4%: EBIT of ₹140.96 crore (pre-tax profit ₹114.91 crore plus finance cost ₹26.05 crore) over capital employed of about ₹1,908 crore (equity ₹1,514.02 crore, borrowings ₹326.06 crore, leases ₹68.36 crore). Removing ₹623.89 crore of cash, bank deposits and investments lifts it to about 11.0% [6]. Four drags explain the gap to the standalone ROCE of 21%: GEML's operating loss of about ₹182 crore, goodwill and intangibles of ₹423.99 crore (about 22% of capital employed), idle treasury cash and the lending book. Standalone ROCE fell from 27% in FY19 to 4% in FY22 and recovered to 21% in FY26 [6]. A core-only ROCE is not disclosed, and it is the number a business-quality judgment needs.

web_blocks.caption: Exceptional items, FY23 to H1 FY27 (₹ crore; negative is a charge; consolidated; annual reports and the Q2 FY27 results)
rows: Impairment of assets under development ₹15.84 crore among other items [8]
FAME provision ₹477.32 crore (refund ₹139.98 crore plus receivable ₹337.34 crore), offset by Pune land gain ₹150.15 crore [8][19]
Labour Codes ₹19.26 crore, e-powertrain project impairment ₹15.98 crore, land-use fee ₹3.58 crore, overseas subsidiary write-off ₹0.52 crore [6]
GEML IPO costs ₹12.66 crore, Bestway goodwill ₹17.6 crore and brand ₹2.49 crore; a further ₹27.30 crore of accelerated depreciation sits above the line (total one-offs ₹60.1 crore in Q2) [2][1]
web_blocks.takeaway: The five periods sum to −₹417.55 crore of net charges (derived), recurring in different forms: a subsidy clawback, impairments, a failed listing and discontinued brands [8][6][2]. Management says there is “nothing more at this stage”, and also that the review is a regular period-end exercise [62]. We treat them as part of the cost of running an EV subsidiary and an acquisition programme, not as true one-offs. FAME is the sharpest case: the ministry alleged breach of local-content rules, GEML refunded ₹139.98 crore without admitting it, and eligibility was partly restored under later schemes [8][33].

web_blocks.text: Contingent liabilities, related parties and auditors. At March 2026 consolidated contingent liabilities were: customs ₹129.44 crore (mainly the Chennai Customs order of 27 January 2024 treating 2018–21 e-scooter imports as kits, ₹56.44 crore duty plus interest and penalty, appeal pending); sales tax ₹43.96 crore; excise ₹26.00 crore; other claims ₹33.73 crore; income tax ₹6.11 crore; wage demands ₹14.45 crore. None is provided; the items total about ₹254 crore (derived) [6]. ALJ is both 37.5% co-owner of GEML and a lender (₹20.30 crore at 10.09%), normal for a joint venture but worth watching [6]. Deloitte signed through FY25 and Price Waterhouse from FY26; the FY26 opinion is unmodified, with goodwill and intangibles impairment (₹211.82 crore and ₹212.17 crore) as the key audit matter, and the Q2 FY27 review is unmodified [6][7][2]. Receivables over three years old (₹84.19 crore) are almost fully provided (₹84.60 crore) [6].

Dilution, rights issue and dividends. Dilution at the listed parent has been small: 23.29 crore shares, one buy-back of 1.30 crore shares in November 2019, and employee options equal to about 1.0% of the fully diluted count [12][67]. The dilution that matters is below the parent. In 2022 Abdul Latif Jameel paid ₹1,170.81 crore for 35.80% of GEML, and the July 2026 rights issue of ₹530 crore (Greaves ₹331.12 crore, ALJ ₹198.87 crore) left holdings near 62.5% and 37.5% [9][2]. Minority holders therefore bear about 37.5% of GEML's losses: FY26 profit attributable to Greaves shareholders was ₹107.14 crore against ₹35.29 crore for the group, and in FY24 −₹135.27 crore against −₹367.27 crore [6][8]. Dividends of ₹2 a share (about ₹46.6 crore a year) totalled about ₹165 crore from FY23 to H1 FY27 (₹4.63, 20.88, 46.50, 46.56 and 46.58 crore), a period in which cumulative operating cash flow was negative [9][8][6][2].

web_blocks.company: Kirloskar Oil Engines and Cummins India, peer engine and genset makers
web_blocks.region_era: India, CPCB IV+ emission transition and commodity spike, 2023–2026
web_blocks.mechanism: A new emission rule adds costly content (exhaust treatment, electronic injection), lifts unit prices and triggers pre-buying, then volumes settle below the old level while metal prices run ahead of contract repricing. Margins whipsaw even when revenue grows, because pricing is set quarterly and costs move daily.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: CPCB IV+ genset volumes ran at 80–85% of CPCB-II levels with price increases of 5–18% [89][90]. In Q2 FY27 Kirloskar's standalone EBITDA margin fell from 14.0% to 11.0% on revenue up 19% [81]; Cummins India revenue rose 4% while pre-tax profit fell 28.4% [83]. Greaves' core margin fell from 14.8% to 11.5% on revenue up 24% [1]. Greaves' group margin has swung 15% (FY17), 1.5% (FY22), 7.0% (FY26) [60][4].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Greaves' earnings are cyclical in margin more than in revenue, so a single year's EBITDA is a poor guide to the through-cycle level. The operating test is whether raw materials return from 67.8% of core revenue toward the 64% of a year earlier as OEM indexation catches up in Q4 FY27 [1][24]. If the pattern holds, the core margin recovers with no help from volume. If it does not, the 2022 precedent shows how far the margin can fall.

web_blocks.title: Genuine cash compounding versus accounting optics
paragraphs: Genuine: a standalone margin of 13–14% for three years, core net cash of ₹110 crore, doubled revenue, a GEML loss per scooter cut from about ₹20,000 to ₹6,300, and receivables older than three years that are almost fully provided [62][1][6].

Optics: a negative cash cycle resting on 92 payable days; owners' profit (₹107.14 crore in FY26) three times the group's because minorities absorb GEML losses; “business PBT” that excludes ₹60.1 crore of Q2 charges; treasury interest income that flatters the pre-tax line; and a lending-adjusted operating cash flow the company does not itself report [1][6][2].

web_blocks.text: Our judgment on earnings quality. The case that earnings are sound: the core produced real operating profit through a hard commodity cycle, carries little debt and reports receivables honestly. The case that they are not: over five years the group produced negative cumulative operating cash flow on ₹619 crore of EBITDA, booked about ₹418 crore of net exceptional charges from FY23 to H1 FY27, and shows ₹60 crore of fresh charges in the latest quarter [60][8][2]. Our weighting is that the core earns genuine cash profit, probably near its 11–15% EBITDA margin over a cycle, while consolidated numbers understate it because GEML's losses and the lender's loan book sit on top. Treat group earnings as low quality until GEML reaches positive EBITDA and operating cash flow turns positive on its own, which management dates only as “fairly soon” and “12 to 18 months” [24]. That is a judgment about the record, and the next chapters ask whether the business is good enough to wait for it.

book_paragraphs: Picture an auditor at a quiet desk in a Pune office, late in the evening, with three statements open side by side. The profit and loss says the company made money. The balance sheet says it owns a lot. The cash flow statement says, in the flattest language accounting allows, that the cash never arrived. You and I are going to read Greaves the way that auditor would, because the quickest way to understand a company is to ask where the cash went.

Let us first agree on the three words that carry this chapter. EBITDA is the profit a business earns from its operations before the cost of its machines wearing out and before interest. Operating cash flow, which we will call CFO, is the cash those operations actually put in the bank after changes in stock, customer credit and supplier credit. Working capital is the money tied up in that stock and credit. A healthy business turns its EBITDA into CFO within a year or two. A business that does not, year after year, is telling you something, however good the profit line looks.

For the first seven years in our table, Greaves did what a healthy business does. From the year to March 2015 to the year to March 2021 it generated about 1,243 crore rupees of operating cash. Its margin was between 11 and 15 percent, it carried no debt for much of the period, and it paid out most of its profit as dividends. Then came a run of bad luck and some bad decisions. A pandemic. New emission rules that forced a redesign of engines. A shortage of chips. A spike in metal prices. In the year to March 2022, operating profit fell to 25 crore rupees, which is 1.5 percent of sales.

The next four years are where the forensics get interesting. In FY23, the company took in about 1,171 crore rupees from Abdul Latif Jameel, which bought a little over a third of the electric subsidiary. It repaid its borrowings and sales jumped 58 percent to 2,699 crore. And yet operating cash flow was negative by 135 crore, because 332 crore had gone into other assets, mostly a subsidy receivable from the government. The company was owed money for scooters sold, and was counting that as revenue before it was collected. In 2023 the government alleged that the subsidiary had not followed the local-content rules, and the receivable was written down. Think about what that does to the word 'profit'.

That write-down, 477 crore rupees including a 140 crore refund, turned a profitable year into a loss of 367 crore. A gain of 150 crore from selling land in Pune softened the blow, but the tax on that gain, 114 crore, made the cash picture worse. Next year the loss was small, and after that a recovery began. In the year to March 2026 operating profit reached 239 crore, its highest since FY19, and the cash flow turned barely positive at 33 crore. In the half-year to September 2026 it went to negative 212 crore. If you stopped there, you would think the company was in trouble.

But look closer, as an auditor would. The company has a lending arm that finances electric scooter buyers. A lender has to hand out the loan before it earns the interest, so as its book grows, cash flows out of operations. In the half-year, about 205 crore rupees went into that book, almost exactly the 206 crore by which loans on the balance sheet grew. Take that out and operating cash flow is about negative 7 crore, close to break-even. Stock grew by 141 crore, but suppliers financed most of it, by 98 crore. So the picture is neither alarming nor reassuring. It is a growing group that is using cash, partly by design.

Now separate the two stories, the way the company itself now does. In the first half of this fiscal year the engine and generator business earned 178 crore rupees of EBITDA on sales of 1,478 crore, a margin of 12 percent. A year earlier it earned 184 crore, or 14.9 percent. Sales rose by a fifth and profit slipped. The scooter business lost 63 crore at the same level, against 78 crore a year earlier. Put the two together, add a small amount from the lender, and the group earned 130 crore. Notice that the group's margin barely moved, around 6 percent, while its two parts moved in opposite directions. A single blended number hid both stories.

Debt tells a similar story. In FY23 the group had almost none; by September 2026 it had about 569 crore, counting leases. Where did it go? At least 193 crore of the March 2026 debt is match-funded, which is a clumsy phrase for a simple idea: the lender borrowed money against loans it made and will repay from the borrowers' instalments, the way a bank does. Another 108 crore is working-capital loans for the scooter maker, and 20 crore is a loan from its minority partner. The engine business itself holds 150 crore of cash against 40 crore of debt. You would not guess that from the consolidated figure.

Is this slip in the core a sign of a weaker business, or of a cycle? Ask the peers. Kirloskar Oil Engines, a rival, saw its standalone margin fall from 14 percent to 11 percent in the same quarter, on sales that were up 19 percent. Cummins India's sales rose 4 percent while its pre-tax profit fell 28 percent. When emission rules force a redesign and metals get dearer faster than contracts reprice, everybody's margin drops, even as revenue climbs. That is a cycle, and Greaves's own history shows how deep one can go: 15 percent in FY17, 1.5 percent in FY22. The test is simple. Do the raw-material costs, now close to 68 percent of core sales, drift back toward the 64 percent of a year ago when contracts catch up, which management expects by the last quarter of this fiscal year?

What about the quality of the profit? Here are some honest observations. Of the 35 crore of profit the group reported for FY26, minority shareholders absorbed a loss of 72 crore, so the shareholders of Greaves themselves earned 107 crore. That is a good number that comes from the scooter maker's partners paying their share of its losses. Charges keep arriving: 39 crore in FY26, then 60 crore in the September 2026 quarter, including a write-off of goodwill on an e-rickshaw acquisition and a brand that was dropped. The finance chief says there is nothing more at this stage. He also says the review happens every quarter. You can believe both and still budget for more.

One more flow deserves your attention: what was paid out and what was put in. The company has paid a dividend of two rupees a share each year, about 47 crore rupees, even in years when operating cash was negative; across FY23 to the latest half-year that is about 165 crore. Over the same period the parent put 331 crore into the scooter maker through a rights issue in July 2026, and its minority partner added 199 crore. A rights issue is a new share sale offered to existing owners in proportion to what they already hold, so the ownership split did not change. What changed is that the business now has the cash for 12 to 18 months of burn, in the finance chief's words. A cash cushion bought with the owners' own money is real, and it is also the price of the last four years.

Return on capital, which asks how much operating profit a company earns on every rupee tied up in it, is the number most readers skip and should not. For FY26, our arithmetic gives about 7.4 percent, or about 11 percent if you strip out the large pool of idle cash. The engine business alone earned 21 percent on its own capital. The gap is the cost of the scooter business, 424 crore of acquired goodwill and intangibles, and treasury cash earning a modest rate. Whether Greaves can close that gap is the whole question for a long-term owner.

There is one last thing to look at, and it is the boring part of the annual report that most people skip. The contingent liabilities, which are claims the company disputes but has not provided for, add up to about 254 crore rupees. The largest is a customs demand of 129 crore, of which the central piece is 56 crore over whether imported scooter parts counted as kits. The auditors, a new firm from FY26, gave a clean opinion and flagged goodwill as the key area of judgment. The scooter maker's partner is also its lender. None of that is an alarm. All of it is the kind of footnote that a patient reader remembers when the next surprise comes.

So what do we conclude? You and I are not looking for a villain. We are looking for the point where words turn into cash. The engine business looks like a sound, cyclical manufacturer that has recovered its margins and carries no real debt. The electric subsidiary looks like a young business that has, at last, started to lose less per scooter and has been funded for another year or so. The consolidated accounts mix the two, add a lender, and make the group look worse on cash than the core would. If management is right, the next 12 to 18 months will show the scooter maker running on its own cash. If it is wrong, the statements will show it first.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Warren Buffett wrote that only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked. In accounts the tide is cash. A year of good profit with weak cash is a swimmer who has not yet been tested. Greaves had five such years, and for most of them the cause was a receivable from a government and a lender growing its book. Ask of every profit: when does this turn into money, and from whom?

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Charlie Munger said that if you show him the incentive, he will show you the outcome. A subsidy is an incentive that the customer, the manufacturer and the regulator all read differently. The FAME episode cost Greaves 477 crore rupees because the rules for earning the subsidy were not the same as the rules for selling a scooter. Today the subsidy is only about 5 percent of an Ampere's selling price, which is a healthier base.

web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
question: Is the profit real cash, and what does the balance sheet say about the last ten years?
